title: Elon's smiling. For the market, the hugest outrageous profi
text:
Elon's smiling. For the market, the hugest outrageous profitability claims are made. For himself, the "stretch" hurdles aren't quite as high. 
Tesla ( TSLA ) just unveiled Elon Musk’s new 10-year CEO performance award plan. The crux of this compensation plan can be summarized by the following presentation schematic (included in the 8-K ):

Elon’s compensation will consist of 12 equity tranches, each equivalent to 1% of Tesla’s outstanding shares today (1.69 million shares). Those tranches vest as the indicated milestones are met. There is:
One market capitalization metric, with 12 different milestones. two operational metrics, revenue and adjusted EBITDA, with eight milestones each. For each tranche to vest, one market capitalization and one operational metric needs to be hit. These seemingly simple and “shareholder aligned” objectives have a tremendous number of implications, which this article will highlight. Let’s start …
EBITDA Doesn’t Matter Much It would seem that with there being an EBITDA milestone, Tesla would finally be paying some attention to profitability. That isn’t really so .
Here’s why: To get each tranche Elon Musk needs Tesla to hit one market cap milestone and one additional operational milestone. Now here’s the funny part. There are two operational milestones, EBITDA and revenues. So in essence this is the same as saying that if revenue is consecutively hit, then EBITDA doesn’t matter!
Since there are only eight revenue milestones and 12 market capitalization milestones, though, full vesting does require ultimately also hitting a few EBITDA milestones. Four of those EBITDA milestones would thus be required to get the final four equity tranches.
Put another way, TSLA would have to get up to $6 billion in EBITDA for Elon to see all tranches ultimately vest. Of note, $6 billion in EBITDA would be more or less what Tesla would need to even justify its current enterprise value, never mind that which it seeks for the future.
The Implied Margins Are Amazingly Low What are the implied EBITDA margins on this otherwise aggressive-looking compensation plan?
On a milestone per milestone basis, the implied adjusted EBITDA margins are as follows:
The first comment is that it would be doubtful that investors would actually be buying Tesla today if they thought 8% EBITDA margin was some kind of long-term achievement.
But it’s worse. Remember, Elon Musk would only have to hit four EBITDA milestones to get to full vesting. So to get full vesting Tesla would only have to produce $6 billion in EBITDA on $175 billion in sales! That’s a 3.4% EBITDA margin . What a stretch target that one is.
Also, this EBITDA is adjusted for stock compensation (which is added back in), making it an easier EBITDA margin still, even though it’s so low to begin with.
Someone Forgot The Profitability Story I don’t know if it was the board or Elon Musk. But someone forgot how Tesla was supposed to become as valuable as Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ). Here’s a reminder from 2015 , as per Elon Musk (bold emphasis is mine):
We’re going to spend staggering amounts of money on capex . I mean, for good reasons, and with a great ROI. And it’s important to not look at capex in isolation, because that capex obviously is being done for reason, in order to capture substantial future revenue flow. I’m just saying the sort of back-of-the-envelope — if you make certain assumptions, and I emphasize these are just certain assumptions… I’m not saying they’re true or they will occur. I bet that they do occur, personally — that’s just my personal opinion. I mean, if you take this year’s revenue around $6 billion or thereabouts, and if we are able to maintain a 30% growth rate for 10 years added to your 10% profitability number and have a 20PE, our market cap would be basically the same as Apple’s is today. Now that’s going to require a bit — on the order of $700 billion. Obviously, getting there will require some significant capex .
But I’m hopeful that we can do this without any significant dilution to the company — maybe minor dilution, but nothing serious.
Since Elon’s multiplying 10% of revenues times price/earnings, this means he’s working with a net profit margin . Net of taxes. Including depreciation. Including interest costs. That 10% is thus a number which would be a small fraction of a corresponding EBITDA margin (20% or more). So what happened that this 20% or more implied EBITDA margin suddenly turned into a 3.4%-8.0% EBITDA stretch target milestone ? It boggles the mind.
The Implied Valuation Makes Little Sense The plan is filled with other amazing implications.
For instance, the terminal market capitalization milestone is $650 billion. The terminal EBITDA milestone is $14 billion. Well, even ignoring debt (to come up with enterprise value, in a very capital intensive business to boot) that would be a massive terminal 46.4x Market cap / EBITDA !
Does this make any sense? By then Tesla would be as large as General Motors (NYSE: GM ) or Ford (NYSE: F ), and thus its growth would no doubt collapse, yet the implied valuation would still be that of a massive grower?
Of course, we again have to remember that Elon Musk only actually has to hit 4 EBITDA milestones. So he needs $6 billion EBITDA tops. At the $650 billion market capitalization milestone, that would be a mind boggling 108.3x Market cap / EBITDA (again, we’re ignoring debt).
Milestones Can Be Hit Issuing Equity For Tesla issuing equity is like breathing. If it stops, it dies. So Tesla has issued equity (and converts) and will issue more. Alas, the most important compensation milestone is that of market capitalization. Market capitalization increases as Tesla issues equity.
Granted, the stock awards are based on the current share count (outstanding, not diluted – smart), so diluting the shareholders also dilutes the compensation somewhat. Anyway, the compensation starts at Elon Musk taking a full 12% of Tesla's existing stock, so diluting that a bit doesn't seem all that problematic.
The Zero Salary Both presently and in the future, Elon Musk won’t be drawing a (cash) salary. This seems an outstanding commitment to the mission. At least until you think about it a bit more. Consider the following:
A salary would deduct from EBITDA and profitability in general. This is the least important factor of all , but Tesla’s horrid profitability is attained even though the CEO doesn’t draw a salary in a world of massively well-compensated CEOs. Since Elon Musk does not draw a salary but has massive expenses, what with all those mansions and actress interests, he does need money to spend. So how does it do it? Debt. Elon Musk borrows against his Tesla shares and spends. Now, here’s the funny thing. Unlike income, money you borrow doesn’t pay income taxes. But you can spend it all the same. The result is that the entire practice is a nice way to avoid paying income taxes on any money spent. Conclusion The new Elon Musk compensation plan is hyping Tesla stock again, what with all the lofty market capitalization milestones. Speculators, in the most overbought market in history, will necessarily think along the lines “Elon Musk hit his previous market capitalization milestones, so he’ll hit the next ones as well.”
Of course, it wasn’t Elon Musk hitting the market capitalization milestones. It was a very believing market which did it for him, even though Tesla is more reliant on external financing now than in the past five years. If and when the market dries up for new Tesla financing, Tesla will have a lot of trouble surviving.
But anyway, the plan itself as we saw contains ludicrous assumptions. The assumptions are massively low on profitability and massively high on valuation. Moreover, the profitability assumptions run directly counter Elon Musk’s prior statements of great riches and margins to come. In a way, the EBITDA milestones on this compensation plan represent a massive drop (60-80% lower) to Tesla’s expected long-term profitability, if we compare them to Elon Musk’s prior comments on long-term profitability .
